Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

vignette: Now fifty-one, Mai Nguyen still remembered how the silence around her had stopped feeling neutral when she was thirty-two. For months, a man had tracked her daily routes, leaving voicemails that were nothing but familiar songs played on a loop, and slipping printed newspaper clippings into her mailbox that featured the same melodies in headlines. The intrusion did not announce itself with violence at first; it arrived through the radio, through television news segments that accidentally cut to the same chord progression she heard in her break room, through the steady, unblinking presence of a police officer who had arrived at her apartment door after her husband's repeated calls. When the officer finally took her statement, his heavy belt and the formal cadence of his questions had done nothing to quiet the ringing in her ears. Instead, the uniform and the procedural rigidity had locked onto the earlier intrusions, cementing the feeling that safety was a paper shield. At the dental clinic where she had built her practice, these tensions took physical form. Mai always positioned her office chair facing the door, then angled it so her back rested firmly against the reinforced wall behind her. She mapped the exam rooms the same way, choosing the corner suite where the reinforced glass allowed her to monitor the hallway while her own seating was shielded from the entrance. When patients asked why she sat so precisely, she explained it as a preference for posture, but what frightened her most was the hollow certainty that no one could guarantee her safety. Even when her husband held her in the evenings and whispered that the man was gone, that she was protected, the words slid over her like water over glass. She needed to feel the wall, needed to see the entire room laid out before her, or the quiet of her own home began to feel like a holding pattern. Over the years, these adjustments accumulated into a rigid routine. She began to flinch when the morning news broadcast a particular pop ballad, her hands tightening around her coffee mug until her knuckles went white. If a grocery store commercial used the same minor-key jingle, she would walk out of the aisle without completing her list. When she drove past a patrol car, even one parked at a quiet intersection, she felt her chest tighten, certain that the officer inside was looking at her not as a citizen, but as a case file. She had come to believe that the world was laced with the same patterns, that the threat was still moving, waiting for the right frequency to announce itself. She stopped letting her staff suggest music in the treatment rooms, citing infection control protocols, though she knew the truth. She avoided scanning local news channels, trading them for silent audiobooks while she sterilized instruments. The habit of choosing exits first, of sitting with her spine pressed to the back of the reception bench during staff meetings, became so entrenched that she no longer questioned it. Her colleagues noticed the precision of her movements, the way she timed her coffee breaks to coincide with shifting shifts, but Mai's internal world was occupied by a different calculus. She was certain that if she relaxed her vigilance, the pattern would resume. It was her husband who finally noticed the cost. He watched her hesitate at the threshold of their dining room, scanning the space twice before pulling out a chair. He saw how she flinched at the sudden chime of her phone, how she avoided the park where patrol cars routinely patrolled. The exhaustion had settled into her shoulders, and the constant orientation toward threat left little room for the quiet years they had planned. Mai came to this office because the vigilance had begun to fray her focus during crown preparations, and because she was tired of waking up already braced. She did not know if the wall behind her could ever truly hold, but she hoped someone might help her understand why the world felt so permeable, and whether the silence could ever mean what it used to.
